Operations & Supply Chain

Supply chain design, process optimization, lean principles, capacity planning, and Six Sigma fundamentals.

Lesson Lectures · learn Data · apply

Marketing wins the sale, but operations decides whether you make money on it. Operations is the engine that turns raw inputs into delivered product — and the whole game is moving work through that engine fast, cheap, and defect-free. This is a hands-on lesson: hover the cards, scan the diagrams, and take the quiz. We'll use the two retail giants — Amazon and Walmart — and their real, latest numbers to make it concrete.

1 · Three levers every operation pulls

Toyota built the most-copied operating system on earth around a single goal: highest quality, lowest cost, shortest lead time. Click each lever to see what it means

"How long from order to cash?" The clock that runs from when a customer places an order to when you collect payment. Most of that time, the product is just waiting, not being worked on. Shrinking the wait is where the money hides.

"What are we paying for that the customer won't?" In Lean, waste is any action that consumes resources without adding value to the customer. Toyota names seven types (TIMWOOD): Transport, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Over-processing, Over-production, Defects.

"Never knowingly pass a defect downstream." Catch and fix problems where they happen instead of repairing finished product later. Stopping the line to fix one defect is cheaper than shipping a thousand bad ones.

"all we are doing is looking at the timeline from when the customer gives us an order to the point at which we collect the cash and we're reducing that timeline by removing non-value added wastes"

— EMS Consulting Group, "Lean Manufacturing: What is Lean and the Toyota Production System?" · in your corpus

2 · The vocabulary — flip to learn

These are the exact words operations managers use on the factory floor and in the warehouse. Hover a card to reveal it.

3 · The Theory of Constraints in one line

If a chain breaks at its weakest link, strengthening any other link is wasted effort. The same is true for a process: output is set by the slowest step.

System throughput  =  capacity of the bottleneck

So improving a non-bottleneck step doesn't raise output — it just piles up work-in-progress in front of the real constraint. Here's a 4-station line making 100 units of demand a day. Click each bar to see its capacity:

In a ballpoint-pen assembly demo, a team cut a job from 90 seconds to 66 seconds — a 50% throughput gain — by re-balancing work, not adding people. First synchronize upstream stations to the bottleneck (kill the work-in-progress pile), then move an idle worker's spare time over to help the constraint. Only if that's not enough do you add cost/resources. Identify → synchronize → redistribute → then add resources.

"the bottleneck is the limiting operation you cannot work faster than the bottleneck and if the previous operations work faster it is of no use because the output does not go up and only WIP builds up in between"

— Shrinivas Gondhalekar, "TOC Theory of Constraints & De bottlenecking" · in your corpus

Bottleneck ≠ constraint (the subtle trap)

A bottleneck is any resource with capacity at or below its demand. The constraint is the one bottleneck that limits the whole system's goal. A plant can have several bottlenecks, but pouring effort into a non-binding one just grows the queue in front of the real constraint — "the plant as a system will have no benefit from this so-called improvement." Always improve the constraint.

4 · Two giants, same revenue, opposite operating models

Here's where operations gets real. Amazon and Walmart booked almost identical revenue last fiscal year — yet they make money in completely different ways. This is the operations manager's core trade-off: fat margin vs. fast turnover.

Net margin (Amazon) = 77.67 ÷ 716.92 = 10.8%. Net margin (Walmart) = 21.89 ÷ 713.16 = 3.1%. Walmart keeps about 3 cents of every sales dollar.

Asset turnover (Walmart) = 713.16 ÷ 284.67 = 2.51× — it generates $2.51 of sales per $1 of assets. Amazon = 716.92 ÷ 818.04 = 0.88×, weighed down by warehouses and AWS data centers.

The punchline — Return on Assets ties out close: margin × turnover = ROA. Amazon: 10.8% × 0.88 ≈ 9.5%. Walmart: 3.1% × 2.51 ≈ 7.7%. A razor-thin grocer competes with a tech-margin giant because operational speed (turnover) substitutes for margin. That's the whole secret of Walmart's model.

5 · Check yourself

A 4-step line has capacities 90, 60, 100, 120 units/hour. What is the line's throughput?

Throughput equals the capacity of the slowest step — the bottleneck at 60. No step can outrun it, and averaging is meaningless here.

A factory keeps 3 months of parts in a warehouse "just in case." Which Lean idea attacks this most directly?

Just-in-Time targets excess inventory — it frees the cash tied up in stock and cuts warehouse cost and obsolescence risk.

Walmart and Amazon earn similar Return on Assets despite very different margins. Walmart pulls this off mainly through…

Walmart's thin 3% margin is rescued by spinning assets 2.51× a year vs Amazon's 0.88×. Speed of turnover substitutes for margin — and it actually holds fewer assets.

One subtlety → your bridge to the next course

Notice the two giants made nearly the same revenue but Amazon holds $818B in assets to Walmart's $285B. Choosing how much capital to sink into warehouses, data centers, and inventory — and whether to own or rent that capacity — is an operations decision that becomes a finance decision. How a firm funds and allocates that asset base is the heart of Capital Allocation and Strategy in the courses ahead.

Your move (the Course 06 output)

Pick any process you touch — your morning routine, a coffee shop line, your team's deploy pipeline. Map the steps, time each one, and circle the slowest (the bottleneck). Then ask the four de-bottlenecking questions in order: can you synchronize upstream steps to it, redistribute idle effort toward it, and only then add resources? Estimate the throughput gain before spending a dollar.

From the Canon — Goldratt, Ohno, Bossidy & Charan, and 4DX

The lesson above gave you the mechanics of flow — bottlenecks, waste, turnover. The canon adds the discipline layer: how to find the one constraint that matters, how Toyota built a culture (not just a toolkit) around eliminating waste, and how to stop the daily whirlwind from quietly strangling the one improvement that would actually move throughput.

Goldratt's deepest move isn't "find the bottleneck" — it's subordinate, don't sprint. Speeding up the steps before the constraint changes nothing but the size of the pile in front of it:

"the bottleneck is the limiting operation — you cannot work faster than the bottleneck, and if the previous operations work faster it is of no use because the output does not go up and only WIP builds up in between"

— Shrinivas Gondhalekar, "TOC Theory of Constraints & De-bottlenecking" · in your corpus

Ohno's lesson is that JIT and "stop the line" only work as a culture — and the andon cord proves the payoff of catching defects at the source rather than shipping them downstream:

"if an irregularity occurs… the worker presses the call button, then a yellow lamp is displayed… if the issue is not resolved within a set distance, the assembly line will stop… the problem is solved even if it means stopping production"

— Toyota Motor Corporation, "The Toyota Production System as Taught by Toyota - Episode 01" · in your corpus

And once you know which constraint to attack, 4DX is the scaffold that keeps the daily firefight from eating the improvement. Its sharpest insight — the one most teams miss — is to drive lead measures, not the lag measure you can see but can't move:

"even the smartest people fall into the Trap of fixating on a lag measure they can't directly influence… because lags are easier to measure and they represent the result we ultimately want"

— Chris McChesney, "The 4 Disciplines of Execution in a Nutshell" · in your corpus

The buffer-less trap — efficiency vs. resilience

Pure JIT trades resilience for efficiency: zero inventory shatters under a supply shock. The corpus is a live case study — a buyer's part jumped from "$150" to "$1800" the instant a carrier and tariff regime shifted, because lean left no cushion to absorb it. Post-2020 the practitioner swing is to just-in-case buffers on critical, single-sourced inputs — Goldratt's "elevate vs. demand" tension playing out in the real world. Lean the flow; insure the chokepoints.

Go deeper in the canon cluster: The Goal, Toyota Production System, Execution, and The 4 Disciplines of Execution — each note carries the full quotes and sourcing.

How Toyota Changed The Way We Make Things signal 1
Bloomberg Originals · 4:52 · 2,298,337 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~852 words

Toyota knows how to make cars. It does it so well it became the first company to produce more than 10 million a year. Its success is rooted in a special system and began what is now known as ‘Lean Manufacturing’, an ethos emulated by companies around the world to make products faster, cheaper and better. Following the Second World War, Japan was left in a precarious economic position. "Steel and other metals are scarce" Already disadvantaged by lacking natural resources, materials were hard to come by and companies had to be creative to compete. Toyota’s founder Sakichi Toyoda had started a loom business, but it was his son Kiichiro who founded the motor company in 1937.

They were used to working within narrow margins - as the shortage of materials increased during the war, the number of headlamps on its Model K truck was reduced to one and it only had brakes on one of the axles. The turning point for Toyota's Production System would come in the early fifties, when Kiichiro's cousin Eiji would travel to the U.S. with a veteran loom machinist, Taiichi Ohno. They visited Ford's River Rouge plant in Michigan and were impressed by the scale of the operation, but knew that in cash-strapped Japan companies didn’t have the resources for such a system; Having months’ worth of stock sitting in a warehouse would tie up precious capital they didn’t have.

Instead, what truly impressed Ohno was a visit to a supermarket, a Piggly Wiggly, according to legend... Japan didn’t really have self-service stores at this point - and he was struck by the way customers could choose exactly what they wanted, when they wanted. He decided to model his production line on a similar idea; With a "supermarket formula," only enough parts were produced in the first phase to replace what was used in the second, and so on. This is where the ‘Just In Time’ system really took shape. Toyota was able to eliminate much of the waste in Ford's system, making smaller numbers of parts to be used when it needed them, allowing the company to operate on a tighter budget.

As part of this Ohno developed ‘Kanban’ - a sign-based scheduling method which shows goods in, goods in production, and goods out. It’s now seen as a precursor to bar codes. Ohno and Toyoda also noticed that American car companies were still employing many of Henry Ford’s early production techniques - They kept operations at full tilt in order to maximize efficiencies of scale, and then repaired defective cars after they rolled off the line. Ohno believed this caused more problems and didn’t encourage workers, or machines, to stop making the mistake. So he placed a cord above every station which any worker could pull to stop the entire assembly if they spotted a problem.

The whole team would work on it, to prevent it from happening again. As teams identified more problems, the number of errors began to drop dramatically. Combined with a culture of continuous, incremental improvement -- called `kaizen' -- the Toyota Production System built a brand known for making reliable and affordable cars. But Toyota was also getting good at producing cars quickly. In 1962, the company had produced one million vehicles. By 1972, they had produced ten million. It was around that time the efficiencies of their factories enabled Toyota to produce a car every 1.6 man hours - much lower than their competitors in the U.S., Sweden and Germany And as the oil crises of the decade sent gas prices higher, cheap-to-run Japanese cars became much more appealing to Americans, whose powerful, but gas-guzzling vehicles suddenly became very expensive to run.

Today, Toyota has made over 250 million vehicles… Others have looked to them to learn the lessons of ‘Lean’- combining craft with mass production, avoiding waste, while striving for constant improvement. Boeing is perhaps the most famous, restructuring a plant to better suit TPS. Intel is another long-time lean ambassador, and is exploring the principles in the context of AI and IoT. A Canadian Hospital even used Toyota’s system to decrease wait times in its ER. The Toyota Production System changed not just how cars are made globally but how we approach making things full stop. It also showed there is always a better way to make a product.

What is Bottleneck Analysis | Explained signal 1
LeanVlog · 2:02 · 22,973 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~355 words

what is bottleneck analysis in today's fast-paced business World companies are always looking for ways to improve their processes and increase efficiency and that's where bottleneck analysis comes in bottleneck analysis is a method used to identify the limiting factor or constraint that is slowing down the performance of a process or system this can be anything from a lack of resources such as time or manpower to a slow machine or outdated equipment by identifying the bottleneck organizations can make improvements to increase the overall efficiency of their processes for example imagine a factory that produces car parts the factory has several production lines Each of which has its own machines and workers but despite having enough machines and workers the overall production of the factory is slow through bottleneck analysis the factory management can identify that the limiting factor is a particular machine that is taking longer to complete its task than the others by upgrading this machine the factory can improve its overall production speed bottleneck analysis is a crucial tool for organizations because it helps them understand the root cause of their problems and make improvements that can lead to increased productivity lower costs and improved customer satisfaction by eliminating bottlenecks companies can streamline their processes reduce waste and increase the efficiency of their operations in conclusion bottleneck analysis is a simple but effective tool for organizations looking to improve their processes and increase efficiency by identifying the limiting factors in their processes companies can make targeted improvements that can lead to increased productivity and success thank you for watching you will find more details in the description
